# Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization

Shayan Talaei ^(†)^(†)thanks: Equal contribution. Correspondence:
{[stalaei](mailto:stalaei@stanford.edu),
[agam2026](mailto:agam2026@stanford.edu),
[asoltan](mailto:asoltan@stanford.edu)}@stanford.edu.
Affiliation: Stanford University    Agam Bhatia¹¹footnotemark: 1
Affiliation: Stanford University    Arshia Soltani
Moakhar¹¹footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Stanford University    Jonas
Hübotter Affiliation: ETH Zürich    Amin Saberi Affiliation: Stanford
University    Azalia Mirhoseini Affiliation: Stanford University

###### Abstract

Many real-world applications require language models to internalize
knowledge that was absent from pretraining, to incorporate continually
updated facts, or to learn new domain skills. Self-distillation has
emerged as a natural approach for this task. A model conditioned on the
source material acts as the teacher, and an unconditioned student is
trained to reproduce the teacher’s behavior closed-book. We propose
Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), an efficient per-token mixed-policy
method for self-distillation. The student generates each rollout by
default, while the teacher intervenes only at positions where its
next-token distribution substantially diverges from the student’s.
Unlike off-policy distillation with teacher-generated prefixes, this
design keeps training rollouts close to the student’s test-time
behavior, while avoiding the low-signal states that fully on-policy
rollouts drift into. In effect, SSD lets the teacher steer the rollout
exactly where the privileged context changes the prediction. On three
closed-book QA benchmarks measuring fact recall, knowledge updates, and
skill acquisition, SSD nearly matches on-policy distillation while using
$`38`$–$`69\%`$ fewer supervised tokens and consistently outperforms
off-policy distillation on the held-out test set. On a forgetting stress
test, SSD retains the most general capability while also achieving the
best in-domain accuracy and using less supervision than the on-policy
baseline. Overall, SSD establishes a new accuracy–efficiency–forgetting
Pareto frontier for self-distillation. Project web page is available at
[ssd-distill.github.io](https://ssd-distill.github.io/).

## 1 Introduction

Practical deployments often require language models to use knowledge
that was absent from pretraining, such as updated facts, new
discoveries, or domain-specific information ([Lewis et al.,
2020](#bib.bib24); [Petroni et al., 2021](#bib.bib33); [Gao et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib9)). A common solution is in-context learning (ICL),
where the relevant information is supplied in the prompt at inference
time ([Brown et al., 2020](#bib.bib4); [Dong et al., 2024](#bib.bib5)).

While effective, this approach has several limitations: it uses context
space, requires careful prompt or retrieval design ([Liu et al.,
2022](#bib.bib28)), and adds per-query inference cost. Models can also
fail to use relevant evidence reliably even when it is present in the
context ([Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib29); [Gao et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib9)). Parametric learning offers a complementary approach
by distilling new knowledge into the model’s weights, where it remains
available without repeatedly retrieving and processing the source
material at inference time.

A large body of work has therefore studied how to move knowledge from
context into the model’s weights ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib43); [Lin
et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)). Self-distillation has emerged as one
powerful tool for this setting ([Snell et al., 2022](#bib.bib37);
[Shenfeld et al., 2026a](#bib.bib35)). The idea is to recast the model’s
ICL capability as training signal, conditioning the same model on the
source material to obtain a more informed token distribution from this
teacher, and then distilling that distribution back into the
unconditioned student. The central difficulty is choosing which rollout
states should carry that distillation signal.

Existing self-distillation methods differ in how they generate training
rollouts, creating a tradeoff between distribution match and learning
signal. We make this tradeoff explicit with the _supervision signal_:
the per-token forward Kullback–Leibler divergence between the teacher’s
and student’s next-token distributions along a rollout ([Kullback &
Leibler, 1951](#bib.bib22)). On-policy rollouts match the student’s
test-time distribution, but are signal-starved: after the student
commits to an early prefix, the teacher is conditioned on that prefix
and can only provide a coherent continuation. Off-policy rollouts
preserve stronger signal by using teacher-generated prefixes, but train
the student on trajectories it will not produce at test time. Both
choices therefore allocate supervision inefficiently. On-policy training
spends it on positions where the teacher has little to add, whereas
off-policy training spends it on states the student will not visit. This
raises our central question: can we preserve the signal of off-policy
rollouts while staying close to the student’s distribution?

This inefficient allocation of supervision signal motivates a method
that uses teacher generation selectively while keeping rollouts close to
the student. We propose Speculative Self-Distillation (SSD), a
compute-efficient, per-token mixed-policy method built around
_inflection tokens_: positions where privileged context substantially
changes the teacher’s next-token distribution relative to the student’s.
In SSD the student generates the rollout by default. At each token
position, SSD compares the teacher’s and student’s next-token
distributions. If the divergence between them exceeds a threshold
$`\tau`$ (we use the Jensen–Shannon divergence ([Lin, 1991](#bib.bib26),
JSD;) in most experiments), the position is marked as an inflection
token and the teacher generates the next token
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
The teacher distribution and distillation loss are still evaluated at
every response position; only the policy that emits the rollout token
changes. The threshold $`\tau`$ provides a single knob that interpolates
between prior approaches: small $`\tau`$ recovers off-policy
distillation, while large $`\tau`$ recovers on-policy distillation
(Section [4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 SSD lies on the accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier ‣ 4.5 SSD becomes mostly on-policy during training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).

![Refer to caption](2611.12016v1/main_figure.png)

Figure 1: Speculative Self-Distillation decoding loop. (1) The student
receives the prompt $`x`$, while the teacher receives both $`x`$ and the
privileged context $`C`$. (2) At each rollout position, both models
propose a next-token distribution conditioned on the jointly decoded
prefix. (3) If the switching divergence $`D_{\mathrm{switch}}`$ between
the two distributions exceeds the threshold $`\tau`$, the teacher
samples the next token; otherwise the student does. The loop continues
until the rollout termination condition is met.

Across three closed-book QA benchmarks, SSD nearly matches on-policy
accuracy while using substantially fewer supervised tokens, reducing
supervised-token usage by $`48\%`$, $`38\%`$, and $`69\%`$ relative to
on-policy self-distillation on Company Memo, Wikipedia, and Science Q&A,
respectively. SSD is $`1.35`$ points below on-policy on Company Memo and
$`0.08`$ and $`0.15`$ points above it on Wikipedia and Science Q&A.
Across 4B, 7B, and 14B models on Science Q&A, SSD achieves at least
on-policy accuracy with $`23`$–$`55\%`$ fewer supervised tokens at the
evaluations reported in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").
Crucially, this efficiency does not come at the expense of the model’s
prior capabilities. On a forgetting stress test that fine-tunes
Qwen2.5-7B on a chemistry split, we measure the mean accuracy change
($`\Delta`$) across six broad benchmarks relative to the base model. In
this setting, SSD forgets less than either baseline while also achieving
the highest in-domain accuracy. Its average general performance drops by
$`1.4`$ points, compared with $`4.5`$ points for on-policy and $`6.6`$
points for off-policy distillation. Compared with on-policy
self-distillation, SSD therefore improves all three axes of accuracy,
forgetting, and efficiency at once in this experiment, rather than
trading one against another. Our contributions are as follows:

- •
  A signal-based diagnosis of the off-policy/on-policy tradeoff. Using
  the per-token teacher–student divergence as a diagnostic for the
  supervision available along a rollout, we show that on-policy
  self-distillation is signal-starved at later positions while
  off-policy rollouts carry signal throughout, accounting for on-policy
  training’s compute inefficiency
  (Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 The Inefficiency of On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ 3 Speculative Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
- •
  Speculative Self-Distillation. We propose SSD, a per-token
  mixed-policy method in which the student generates by default and the
  teacher takes over only at _inflection positions_ where the
  teacher–student divergence exceeds a threshold $`\tau`$. A single
  $`\tau`$ interpolates between off-policy ($`\tau\!\to\!0`$) and
  on-policy ($`\tau\!\to\!\infty`$) self-distillation
  (Section [3](#S3 "3 Speculative Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
- •
  On-policy accuracy at a fraction of the supervision. Across three
  knowledge-acquisition tasks (private documents, Wikipedia knowledge
  updates, and scientific Q&A), SSD nearly matches on-policy
  self-distillation accuracy using $`38`$–$`69\%`$ fewer supervised
  tokens. We also show that a sweep over $`\tau`$ traces the
  accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier between the off-policy and
  on-policy endpoints
  (Section [4](#S4 "4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
- •
  Reduced forgetting without sacrificing in-domain accuracy. On a
  forgetting stress test, SSD retains the most general capability while
  achieving the highest in-domain accuracy and using less supervision
  than the on-policy baseline
  (Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 SSD reduces forgetting relative to on-policy methods ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).

## 2 A Unified View of Self-Distillation

Let $`\mathcal{D}`$ be a distribution over pairs $`(C,x)`$, where $`x`$
is the prompt and $`C`$ is the privileged context: a document,
instruction, reference answer, or other information useful for answering
$`x`$. Self-distillation defines a student $`\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$
and teacher
$`\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x,C):=\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}}(\cdot\mid x,C)`$,
which has the privileged information $`C`$ in context and uses the
initial model weights $`\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}`$. The goal of
_self-distillation_ is to update $`\theta`$ so that $`\pi_{\theta}`$
approximates $`\pi_{T}`$ for held-out pairs $`(C^{\prime},x^{\prime})`$,
without $`C^{\prime}`$ being supplied at test time ([Snell et al.,
2022](#bib.bib37)).

#### The self-distillation loss.

The methods we study use the same token-level objective below and differ
only in how rollouts are generated:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{L}(\theta)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\boldsymbol{\pi_{\mathrm{gen}}}}\!\left[\frac{1}{|y|}\sum_{t}D_{\mathrm{loss}}\!\bigl(\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x,C,y_{<t})\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\bigr)\right],
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\pi_{\mathrm{gen}}`$ is the rollout policy and
$`D_{\mathrm{loss}}`$ is a divergence between the teacher and student
next-token distributions. We use the forward KL divergence,
$`D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{T}\,\|\,\pi_{\theta})`$, in our experiments. The
choice of $`\pi_{\mathrm{gen}}`$ defines different methods.

#### Off-policy self-distillation.

Setting $`\pi_{\mathrm{gen}}=\pi_{T}`$ gives off-policy
self-distillation. The teacher generates the response, and the student
is trained to match the teacher along teacher-generated
trajectories ([Snell et al., 2022](#bib.bib37); [Kujanpää et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21); [Eyuboglu et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)). This approach is
simple and data-efficient: every training position lies on a
teacher-generated trajectory with privileged-context guidance. However,
during training the student is supervised on teacher-induced states; at
test time it must act on states induced by its own generations ([Ross
et al., 2011](#bib.bib34)).

#### On-policy self-distillation.

Setting $`\pi_{\mathrm{gen}}=\pi_{\theta}`$ gives on-policy
self-distillation. The student generates the response, while the teacher
provides token-level supervision along the resulting student trajectory
via
Eq. ([1](#S2.E1 "In The self-distillation loss. ‣ 2 A Unified View of Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")) ([Agarwal
et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Shenfeld et al., 2026a](#bib.bib35)). This
removes the train-test mismatch.

#### Dense supervision versus rollout intervention.

Throughout this paper, every response position contributes the
distillation loss in
Eq. ([1](#S2.E1 "In The self-distillation loss. ‣ 2 A Unified View of Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")),
regardless of whether the teacher or student emitted the corresponding
rollout token. The rollout policy therefore controls the *states on
which dense supervision is applied*; it does not decide whether the
teacher is evaluated or whether the loss is present. This distinction is
central to interpreting both the method and its efficiency.

Figure 2: Comparison of off-policy and on-policy training on the
Wikipedia task described in
Section [4](#S4 "4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").
Left: Off-policy training converges faster than on-policy training, but
saturates at lower performance. Middle: Off-policy training has a larger
initial self-distillation loss than on-policy training and converges
faster. Right: We measure the average per-token self-distillation loss
across different token positions within a rollout. We find that a
teacher conditioned on student-sampled prefixes predicts much like the
student itself. This reduces the supervision signal at later positions
of the rollout. Shaded bands (right panel) are 90% bootstrap intervals
of the mean.

## 3 Speculative Self-Distillation

We propose an alternative variant of self-distillation, called
*speculative self-distillation* (SSD), that is more efficient than
on-policy training while achieving better performance than off-policy
training. We first study the tradeoff between off-policy and on-policy
training in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 The Inefficiency of On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ 3 Speculative Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
before introducing SSD in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Method: Switching to the Teacher at Inflection Positions ‣ 3 Speculative Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").

### 3.1 The Inefficiency of On-Policy Self-Distillation

To study the tradeoff between off-policy and on-policy
self-distillation, we compare them on the *Wikipedia* knowledge
acquisition task described in
Section [4](#S4 "4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Dense supervision versus rollout intervention. ‣ 2 A Unified View of Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization") (left)
shows a clear pattern: off-policy training reaches $`78\%`$ accuracy
with roughly $`5\times`$ fewer supervised tokens than on-policy
training, while on-policy training reaches better final performance (run
details in
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Supervision-signal measurements ‣ Appendix C Additional Analyses ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
This is consistent with prior work on on-policy distillation ([Agarwal
et al., 2024](#bib.bib1); [Shenfeld et al., 2026a](#bib.bib35)). The
usual explanation is that on-policy training avoids train-test mismatch.
We focus on the complementary question: *why is off-policy training so
much more compute-efficient?*

1) Off-policy training gives stronger supervision. The loss in
Eq. ([1](#S2.E1 "In The self-distillation loss. ‣ 2 A Unified View of Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"))
measures how much the teacher and student disagree at a training state,
and it also sets the size of the update. We refer to it as the
supervision signal. A larger signal means a larger update, though not
necessarily a more useful one (see point 2 below).
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Dense supervision versus rollout intervention. ‣ 2 A Unified View of Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization") (middle)
shows that off-policy training starts with a substantially larger signal
than on-policy training and also reduces it at a faster rate.

2) On-policy training spends supervision on transient states.
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 The Inefficiency of On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ 3 Speculative Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
illustrates a rollout containing several positions where the teacher and
student strongly disagree. The prompt asks about the “marketing team of
the company”. While the first few response tokens are plausible under
both student and teacher, rollouts of student and teacher diverge at the
fourth token. The teacher begins to discuss the leadership of the
marketing team which is described in its privileged context whereas the
student provides a generic description. We call such a position where
student and teacher disagree strongly an *inflection position*:

###### Definition 1 ($`\tau`$-inflection position).

Given a rollout $`y\sim\pi_{\mathrm{gen}}`$ and $`\tau>0`$, we call the
$`t`$-th position in $`y`$ a *$`\tau`$-inflection position* if

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\delta_{t}\;:=\;D_{\mathrm{switch}}\!\bigl(\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x,C,y_{<t})\,\big\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\bigr)>\tau,
``` |  | (2) |

where $`D_{\mathrm{switch}}`$ is any divergence between the two
next-token distributions.

At an inflection position, the distillation loss heavily pushes the
student away from the original student’s next-token prediction. If the
student later reaches the same prefix, it is likely to choose a
different continuation. For example, in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 The Inefficiency of On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ 3 Speculative Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"),
the student will eventually learn to discuss the “leadership of the
marketing team”. Several states reached by the original student rollout
after the inflection position are therefore transient: they were
produced by a policy that the update is explicitly changing. Supervision
on those states is consequently less useful. In contrast, off-policy
sampling provides detailed information about the marketing team within a
single rollout.

![Refer to caption](2611.12016v1/influence_positions.png)

Figure 3: Example rollout with SSD versus on-policy sampling. Both
rollouts share the prefix “Marketing team is”. At the next token the
teacher and student disagree strongly, which makes it an inflection
position (circled in red). SSD (top) lets the teacher write this token
and a few later ones (orange), and the student writes the rest (blue).
The on-policy rollout (bottom) keeps the student’s token, and the tokens
that follow (gray) are transient states that future rollouts are
unlikely to revisit.

3) The on-policy signal decays quickly along the rollout.
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Dense supervision versus rollout intervention. ‣ 2 A Unified View of Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization") (right)
shows where the supervision goes. Along on-policy rollouts, the signal
is high for the first few tokens and then drops, while along off-policy
rollouts it stays high throughout. The student writes without the
privileged context, so after a few tokens its rollout tends to drift
into generic text that the context says little about. Conditioned on
such a prefix, the teacher mostly agrees with the student and has little
to correct. A teacher-written rollout instead stays tied to the context,
so the teacher keeps disagreeing with the student at later positions.
The same pattern holds on Science Q&A
(Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Supervision-signal measurements ‣ Appendix C Additional Analyses ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")):
the signal in the first quarter of an on-policy rollout is $`3.3\times`$
that of the last quarter, and beyond position 512 it is $`17\times`$
lower than at positions 5–8. On-policy training therefore applies its
loss at every position, but most of that loss falls on states where the
teacher has little to teach.

### 3.2 Method: Switching to the Teacher at Inflection Positions

The previous section highlights a key tradeoff: Off-policy
self-distillation is compute-efficient because teacher trajectories
provide strong supervision, but it trains the student on states it may
not visit at test time. On-policy self-distillation avoids this mismatch
by sampling from the student, but much of its supervision is weak or
spent on transient states. We want the best of both: rollouts should
stay on the student’s distribution when the student is already aligned
with the teacher, and switch to the teacher only where the privileged
context substantially changes the next-token distribution.

This motivates *speculative self-distillation* (SSD): generate from the
student, but let the teacher take over at inflection positions where the
teacher and student strongly disagree. At an inflection position (i.e.,
where $`\delta_{t}>\tau`$), the teacher generates the next token;
otherwise, the student does. The *switching threshold* $`\tau`$ controls
how often the teacher writes the token: lower values hand over to the
teacher more often, while higher values keep rollouts closer to the
student. Training uses
Eq. ([1](#S2.E1 "In The self-distillation loss. ‣ 2 A Unified View of Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"))
with the mixed rollout policy $`\pi_{\mathrm{gen}}=\pi_{\mathrm{mix}}`$
induced by this rule. The switching divergence $`D_{\mathrm{switch}}`$,
together with $`\tau`$, determines which model emits each token, while
$`D_{\mathrm{loss}}`$ defines the distillation loss applied at every
response position. In our experiments, $`D_{\mathrm{loss}}`$ is the
forward KL divergence from teacher to student.

Crucially, the teacher distribution is computed at every response
position in order to evaluate the routing test, and
Eq. ([1](#S2.E1 "In The self-distillation loss. ‣ 2 A Unified View of Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"))
is also applied at every response position. The switch changes only
which policy emits $`y_{t}`$. It should therefore be understood as
selective *trajectory correction*, not selective supervision.

## 4 Experiments and Results

We first describe our experimental setup
(Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")),
then show that SSD nearly matches on-policy self-distillation accuracy
while using $`38`$–$`69\%`$ fewer supervised tokens
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
We then show that these token savings shorten end-to-end training
(Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 SSD’s token savings translate into faster training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"))
and that SSD reduces forgetting compared to both off-policy and
on-policy baselines
(Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 SSD reduces forgetting relative to on-policy methods ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
Finally, we examine how teacher intervention declines during training
(Section [4.5](#S4.SS5 "4.5 SSD becomes mostly on-policy during training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"))
and how the switching threshold controls the accuracy–efficiency
tradeoff
(Section [4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 SSD lies on the accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier ‣ 4.5 SSD becomes mostly on-policy during training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

Tasks. The first task, *Company Memo*, uses a synthetic internal
document about a fictional company, modeling private organizational
knowledge that does not appear online. The second task, *Wikipedia*,
uses articles about natural-disaster events that are available on the
web but happened after the model’s knowledge cutoff date. The third
task, *Science Q&A*, is built from the Chemistry Level-3 subset of
SciKnowEval ([Feng et al., 2025](#bib.bib7)), which contains
undergraduate-level chemistry questions requiring scientific reasoning.
All three tasks are drawn from the experiments in SDFT ([Shenfeld
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib35)).

Models. Unless stated otherwise, the student and the teacher are both
Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. The forgetting study in
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 SSD reduces forgetting relative to on-policy methods ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
uses Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

Baselines. The baselines span the two ends of the self-distillation
spectrum. For off-policy distillation ([Snell et al., 2022](#bib.bib37);
[Eyuboglu et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)), we evaluate SFT, which applies
cross-entropy to teacher-sampled tokens, and FKL, which applies the
forward KL divergence between teacher and student. For on-policy
distillation, we evaluate SDFT ([Shenfeld et al., 2026a](#bib.bib35)).
Hyperparameters for every method, including the switch and threshold of
SSD, are selected on the held-out split
(Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Hyperparameter search ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).

Evaluation. The headline Qwen3-4B comparisons use three independent
training seeds and greedy evaluation. Curves show the mean and $`\pm 1`$
sample standard deviation across seeds. Other experiments use the
evaluation protocols specified in their captions and appendix sections.

Per-task split sizes, hyperparameter searches, prompt templates, and
other implementation details are reported in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").
We include a qualitative case study in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Case Study: JSD-Routed Inference on SciKnowEval Chemistry-L3 ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").

### 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens

Figure 4: SSD approaches or exceeds the on-policy plateau with a
fraction of the supervised tokens. Test accuracy versus cumulative
supervised tokens on Company Memo (left), Wikipedia (middle), and
Science Q&A (right). Each curve is the mean over three independent
training seeds; shading is $`\pm 1`$ sample standard deviation. Each
panel compares the stronger off-policy baseline (SFT or FKL), the
on-policy baseline (SDFT), and SSD. Arrows show the reduction in
supervised tokens from the highest-accuracy on-policy point to the first
SSD point that reaches that accuracy. For Company Memo, we use SSD’s
highest-accuracy point instead.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | On-policy |  | SSD |  |  |

We first evaluate whether per-token switching improves the
accuracy–efficiency tradeoff relative to purely off-policy or on-policy
self-distillation.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
reports test accuracy as a function of cumulative supervised tokens
across our evaluation tasks. Supervised tokens count response positions
that receive the distillation loss, summed over training
(Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1 "Supervised tokens. ‣ B.2 Datasets, evaluation, and supervised-token accounting ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
The Science Q&A curves against training time are in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 SSD’s token savings translate into faster training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").
The baselines exhibit a consistent tradeoff: off-policy training
improves rapidly but plateaus below SSD and on-policy on Wikipedia and
Science Q&A, while on Company Memo it ends close to SSD. On-policy
training reaches a higher plateau only after substantially more
supervision. SSD combines the favorable parts of both regimes. On
Company Memo and Science Q&A, it follows the steep early trajectory of
off-policy training, and on Wikipedia and Science Q&A it continues
improving into the on-policy high-accuracy regime instead of flattening
at the off-policy ceiling.

Relative to on-policy training, SSD uses $`48\%`$, $`38\%`$, and
$`69\%`$ fewer supervised tokens on Company Memo, Wikipedia, and Science
Q&A, with accuracy changes of $`-1.35`$, $`+0.08`$, and $`+0.15`$
percentage points, respectively. SSD therefore stays within $`1.4`$
points of on-policy accuracy on every task. For both token and
training-time comparisons, we use the highest accuracy on the on-policy
mean curve and the first point on the SSD mean curve to reach or exceed
it. If SSD never reaches that accuracy, as on Company Memo, we use its
highest-accuracy point instead. We compute both accuracy differences and
token savings from these pairs, with token savings measured relative to
on-policy training.

This pattern is consistent with the central hypothesis behind SSD. The
useful training signal is concentrated at positions where the privileged
context changes the next-token distribution, while many other positions
can remain student-sampled. By intervening only at those positions, SSD
preserves much of the token efficiency of off-policy training while
retaining the final-accuracy advantage of on-policy training.

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
connects the Science Q&A result to larger models. In all three models,
SSD achieves at least on-policy accuracy with $`23`$–$`55\%`$ fewer
total supervised tokens at the reported evaluations. On the same task,
closed-book SSD also matches or exceeds retrieving solved demonstrations
at inference time while producing shorter responses
(Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Retrieved-demonstration comparison ‣ Appendix C Additional Analyses ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"),
Table [9](#A3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ C.2 Retrieved-demonstration comparison ‣ Appendix C Additional Analyses ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).

### 4.3 SSD’s token savings translate into faster training

Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
showed that SSD nearly matches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised
tokens. Whether this also shortens end-to-end training depends on the
system around it: the trainer and inference engine, the hardware, and
how teacher and student generation are scheduled. A naive implementation
pays for an extra teacher forward pass at every decoding step. We
instead modified vLLM to run the teacher and the student concurrently,
with the teacher on a second GPU sending only its final hidden state to
the student at each step
(Appendix [B.7](#A2.SS7 "B.7 Paired teacher–student inference engine ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
In our training runs, this joint decoding reaches about 92% of the
throughput of student-only decoding, so a joint step takes about as long
as a student step. With this setup, SSD and on-policy training take
nearly the same wall time per million supervised tokens
(Appendix [B.8](#A2.SS8 "B.8 Training time per supervised token ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
Translated into end-to-end training time on Science Q&A, this means that
SSD reaches the on-policy accuracy plateau after about 130 minutes,
while on-policy training needs about 414 minutes, a $`69\%`$ reduction
(Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 SSD’s token savings translate into faster training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
This shows that the token savings of SSD carry over to faster end-to-end
training.

Figure 5: SSD reaches on-policy accuracy in less training time. Test
accuracy versus training time on Science Q&A. Curves show mean $`\pm 1`$
SD over three independent training seeds. Evaluation time is excluded.
Appendix [B.8](#A2.SS8 "B.8 Training time per supervised token ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
reports the training-time breakdown per supervised token.

### 4.4 SSD reduces forgetting relative to on-policy methods

Beyond accuracy and efficiency, self-distillation should preserve the
student’s prior capabilities. Since on-policy self-distillation improves
the accuracy–forgetting tradeoff over supervised fine-tuning ([Shenfeld
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib35)), we evaluate whether SSD preserves this
advantage while selectively using teacher-generated rollout tokens. We
first evaluated forgetting with Qwen3-4B, but observed little separation
between methods: the six-benchmark averages remained close to the base
model across all training methods, which we suspect is due to heavy
post-training toward these benchmarks. To study a setting where
forgetting is induced, we follow [Shenfeld et al. (2026a)](#bib.bib35)
and fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B on the SciKnowEval Chemistry split, measuring
in-domain Science Q&A accuracy (SciQA) against the mean accuracy change
across six general benchmarks ($`\Delta`$).
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
reproduces the off-policy vs. on-policy gap: Off-policy (SFT) and
Off-policy (FKL) acquire the new skill but forget the most
($`\Delta\approx-6.6`$), while On-policy forgets less
($`\Delta=-4.47`$). SSD improves on this tradeoff, achieving the highest
SciQA accuracy ($`73.5\pm 1.7`$), the lowest forgetting
($`\Delta=-1.38`$), and fewer supervised tokens than On-policy
($`2.20`$M vs. $`2.84`$M). This suggests that mixed-policy supervision
can improve the accuracy, forgetting, and efficiency tradeoff
simultaneously.

### 4.5 SSD becomes mostly on-policy during training

Figure 6: Teacher contribution decays over training without an external
schedule. Training dynamics of SSD on Company Memo for four JSD
thresholds $`\tau`$. (Left) Fraction of rollout tokens generated by the
teacher, which drops from up to 43% early in training to 1–5% by the
end. (Right) Mean response length, which is initially longer for higher
thresholds and converges across thresholds as training proceeds.

A desirable switching rule should not require a hand-designed schedule
for how much the teacher participates.
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.5 SSD becomes mostly on-policy during training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
shows that SSD exhibits this behavior automatically. Early in training,
the teacher contributes frequently, especially at lower JSD thresholds,
indicating that the student and teacher disagree at many rollout
positions. As training proceeds, teacher contribution decays across all
thresholds. This decline shows that the switch fires less often as the
student internalizes the privileged-context behavior, shifting the
rollout increasingly toward the student.

The response-length dynamics follow the same adaptation. Runs with
higher thresholds initially produce longer and more variable responses,
reflecting the fact that the student retains control for longer, letting
its draft drift further from the teacher’s distribution. As training
progresses, response lengths stabilize and converge across thresholds.
Thus, SSD does not only reduce teacher usage; it also changes the
distribution of generated trajectories as the student improves. Overall,
teacher control in SSD is high when the student lacks the relevant
knowledge, then naturally recedes as the student becomes competent.

### 4.6 SSD lies on the accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier

In
Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.5 SSD becomes mostly on-policy during training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"),
we evaluate whether the switching threshold $`\tau`$ of SSD effectively
interpolates between off-policy and on-policy self-distillation. Low
thresholds $`\tau\to 0`$ lie near the off-policy endpoint: the teacher
intervenes often, supervised-token usage is low, and final accuracy is
limited. As $`\tau`$ increases, SSD becomes more student-sampled, moving
toward the on-policy endpoint and improving final accuracy. When using
JSD as $`D_{\mathrm{switch}}`$, this divergence is upper bounded by
$`\ln(2)\approx 0.69`$, and hence, any larger $`\tau`$ reduces to
on-policy training. We find in
Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.5 SSD becomes mostly on-policy during training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
that SSD occupies a Pareto frontier: intermediate thresholds achieve
higher accuracy than off-policy training while using fewer supervised
tokens than on-policy training. An ablation of the switching rule
itself, comparing JSD and KL switches with token-level rules from prior
work, is in
Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Switching-rule ablation ‣ Appendix C Additional Analyses ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").

Figure 7: SSD occupies the accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier across
switching thresholds $`\tau`$. Downstream QA accuracy versus cumulative
supervised tokens for Qwen3-4B on Company Memo.

## 5 Related Work

Knowledge distillation and rollout policies. Knowledge distillation
trains a student model to match a teacher’s outputs ([Hinton et al.,
2015](#bib.bib11)) and is a standard mechanism for transferring
language-model capabilities ([Song & Zheng, 2026](#bib.bib38)). One
important design choice is how training trajectories are generated.
Off-policy distillation uses teacher-generated sequences, giving
high-quality supervision but creating a mismatch between training
prefixes and the prefixes the student will produce at test time, a form
of exposure bias studied in imitation learning and sequence
prediction ([Ross et al., 2011](#bib.bib34); [Bengio et al.,
2015](#bib.bib3)). On-policy distillation uses student-generated
sequences and asks the teacher to supervise them ([Gu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10); [Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025](#bib.bib30)),
reducing this mismatch but spending teacher supervision on many tokens
where the teacher provides little new information. Mixed-policy methods
trade off these costs. GKD mixes teacher and student rollouts at the
sequence level ([Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib1)), following earlier
ideas from DAgger, scheduled sampling, and imitation knowledge
distillation ([Ross et al., 2011](#bib.bib34); [Bengio et al.,
2015](#bib.bib3); [Lin et al., 2020](#bib.bib25)). Other methods make
switching decisions within a sequence: SKD lets the teacher replace
student proposals that fall outside the teacher’s top-$`k`$ tokens ([Xu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)), AdaSwitch switches to the teacher after a
sliding-window KL threshold is exceeded ([Peng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib32)), and SWITCH applies a per-position divergence
criterion ([Koo et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)). These works show that
rollout policy is a central lever in distillation, but they study
ordinary two-model distillation; we bring this mixed-policy view to
privileged-context self-distillation.

Context distillation and self-distillation. In context distillation, the
teacher and student share the same base model, but the teacher is given
privileged context that the student will not receive at test
time ([Snell et al., 2022](#bib.bib37)). This context may be a document,
instruction, hint, or retrieved passage, and the goal is to internalize
the resulting behavior into the model’s parameters. Off-policy variants
train on responses generated with privileged context ([Kujanpää et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21); [Eyuboglu et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)), while on-policy
variants supervise student-generated trajectories using the
context-conditioned model ([Shenfeld et al., 2026a](#bib.bib35); [Ye
et al., 2026](#bib.bib44); [Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib45); [Hübotter
et al., 2026](#bib.bib13); [Kleine Buening et al., 2026](#bib.bib19);
[Penaloza et al., 2026](#bib.bib31)). Closest to our setting,
GATES ([Stein et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)) also makes privileged-context
self-distillation selective, but uses agreement among
context-conditioned tutor rollouts to gate which questions and tutor
trajectories are distilled, rather than which policy generates the
rollout. Related work also compresses context into latent state rather
than model weights: Cartridges learns compact document-specific
representations, while Fast KV Compaction constructs compact KV caches
that preserve the attention behavior of the full context ([Eyuboglu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib6); [Zweiger et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)). Recent
on-policy self-distillation methods report better generalization to
held-out questions than off-policy training ([Shenfeld et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib35)), suggesting that staying close to the student’s
test-time distribution is important for robust knowledge acquisition.
However, these methods still commit to generating the full rollout from
the student, even though privileged context typically changes the
next-token distribution only at a small number of knowledge-bearing
positions. We instead ask whether the rollout policy itself can be
chosen selectively at the token level.

Selective use of privileged information. Together, these two lines of
work motivate keeping self-distillation trajectories close to the
student while allowing teacher intervention where privileged context
provides useful information. In knowledge acquisition, this information
may be concentrated at a few knowledge-bearing positions, while many
tokens express syntax, formatting, or reasoning shared by the teacher
and student. Prior work exploits related forms of sparsity through
token-level switching ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Peng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib32); [Koo et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)), token-level
adaptation of the distillation loss ([Jung et al., 2025](#bib.bib16);
[Huang et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Jang et al., 2026](#bib.bib14)), and
context compression that preserves prompt content most relevant to model
predictions ([Zweiger et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)). Evidence from
student-rollout distillation on unseen prompts ([Agarwal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1); [Shenfeld et al., 2026a](#bib.bib35)) and KL-based
analyses of post-training behavior ([Shenfeld et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib36)) further supports keeping training close to the
student’s distribution. These findings motivate SSD, a per-token
mixed-policy method in which the student generates by default and the
context-conditioned teacher intervenes when its next-token distribution
differs substantially from the student’s.

## 6 Conclusion

Self-distillation for closed-book knowledge acquisition faces a tradeoff
between matching the student’s test-time distribution and obtaining
useful supervision from teacher-generated trajectories. We introduced
SSD, which addresses this tradeoff token by token, letting the student
generate by default and switching to the teacher at inflection
positions. Across three closed-book QA tasks spanning private documents,
knowledge updates, and scientific Q&A, SSD nearly matches on-policy
accuracy while using $`38`$–$`69\%`$ fewer supervised tokens. On Science
Q&A, it also reaches the on-policy plateau in about $`69\%`$ less
training time. Varying the switching threshold $`\tau`$ traces an
accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier between off-policy and on-policy
training, while teacher intervention declines automatically as training
progresses. Together with reduced forgetting, these results support
adaptive token-level rollout policies for efficient knowledge
acquisition.

## Appendix A Limitations, Future Work, and Broader Impacts

### A.1 SSD and other axes of the self-distillation pipeline

The comparisons in this paper hold several design choices of the
self-distillation pipeline fixed so that the rollout policy is the only
variable. Each of those choices is itself an active research direction,
and how SSD composes with them remains open. For example, we treat the
QA distribution $`\mathcal{D}`$ as given, whereas [Asawa et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib2) show that document-grounded distillation becomes
substantially more sample-efficient when questions target the parts of
the document the student is most uncertain about. A more deliberate
$`\mathcal{D}`$ would reshape the per-position signal landscape and
therefore the off-/on-policy tradeoffs.

### A.2 Self-distillation for long-horizon and reasoning tasks

Recent work ([Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib18); [Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib42)) has shown that on-policy self-distillation can be
less effective on reasoning-type tasks. In particular, the information
asymmetry between teacher and student means that supervising the student
to match the teacher’s confidence at every position kills the *epistemic
uncertainty* that the student needs to reason its way through the
rollout. We hypothesize that an SSD-like idea can help with this issue
by anchoring the rollout to the teacher only at the critical points of
long sequential dependencies and letting the student carry the rest,
where a fully on-policy method would have to learn each of those
critical points one at a time. Our experiments here are limited to
closed-book QA tasks with relatively short answers, which leaves the
efficacy of SSD on reasoning-heavy tasks underexplored. Verifying it on
these benchmarks is a natural next step.

### A.3 Broader impacts

SSD lowers the cost of internalizing new knowledge into a model’s
weights. As a more efficient form of self-distillation, its broader
impacts are otherwise those of the self-distillation methods it builds
on.

## Appendix B Experimental Details

This section gives the details needed to reproduce our experiments. We
first describe the prompt templates, the datasets, evaluation protocol
and supervised-token accounting, the hyperparameter search, and the
training infrastructure. We then give the settings of the larger-model
scaling runs and the forgetting experiment, followed by the paired
teacher–student inference engine and a breakdown of training time per
supervised token.

### B.1 Prompt templates

The student and teacher both receive the same user question. The teacher
additionally receives a privileged context block placed immediately
before the user question. The privileged context for the teacher is the
question together with its ground-truth answer. This pairing gives the
teacher the complete and minimal information needed to answer the
question, turning the teacher into a near-oracle whose token
distribution the student can usefully imitate. The student sees only the
question, so distillation transfers the answer content into the
student’s weights rather than into a retrieval prompt.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.2 Datasets, evaluation, and supervised-token accounting

For Company Memo and Wikipedia, we use the same set of Question-Answer
pairs released by SDFT ([Shenfeld et al., 2026a](#bib.bib35)). Company
Memo is a synthetic internal document about Hearthwell & Sons
Cooperative, modeling private organizational knowledge that does not
appear online. For Wikipedia, we use the article on Cyclone Ditwah from
the SDFT-released set, on which the base model Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507
scores below $`20\%`$, indicating that it does not possess the article’s
knowledge in its weights. For Science Q&A, we use the Chemistry-L3
subset of SciKnowEval ([Feng et al., 2025](#bib.bib7)). This benchmark
consists of undergraduate-level chemistry multiple-choice questions. The
model must choose among four options and output its final answer in the
format \<answer\>X\</answer\>, which is evaluated against the
ground-truth choice. This setting tests whether self-distillation can
internalize domain-specific scientific knowledge and apply it to
closed-book questions that require short-form reasoning. Under the
$`1024`$-token generation cap used in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"),
the untrained Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 scores $`12.8\%`$ on the Science
Q&A held-out set (the origin of the Science Q&A curves), whereas with a
$`16384`$-token cap it scores $`49.9\%`$
(Table [9](#A3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ C.2 Retrieved-demonstration comparison ‣ Appendix C Additional Analyses ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
We evaluate model answers on Company Memo and Wikipedia with
Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as an LLM judge, decoded greedily (temperature
$`=0`$), using the same evaluation prompt as SDFT ([Shenfeld et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib35)). The judge is the base checkpoint, never a
fine-tuned one, and it is identical for every method, so differences
between methods are scored by the same fixed judge.

For the off-policy distillation methods, we augment each dataset with
teacher-generated answers, sampled from the teacher prompt template
(Section [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Prompt templates ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"))
where the privileged context is the question together with its gold
answer. Targets are sampled once per run (temperature $`1.0`$,
top-$`k=20`$) and reused on every epoch. Their sampling time is included
in the wall-clock comparison in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 SSD’s token savings translate into faster training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").

Train and held-out split sizes per task are summarized in
Table [3](#A2.T3 "Table 3 ‣ B.2 Datasets, evaluation, and supervised-token accounting ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").

|                            |       |      |
|----------------------------|-------|------|
| Task                       | Train | Test |
| Company Memo               | 1133  | 100  |
| Wikipedia (Cyclone Ditwah) | 1129  | 100  |
| Science Q&A                | 2674  | 507  |

Table 3: Number of Train and Test set Question-Answer pairs per task.

#### Supervised tokens.

We count supervised tokens across all training examples and optimizer
steps, excluding prompt tokens, padding, and evaluation. For off-policy
training, a reused teacher target contributes to the count on every
pass. For SSD, both student- and teacher-generated response tokens count
because both receive the distillation loss.

### B.3 Hyperparameter search

All runs fine-tune Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with AdamW, a warmup ratio of
$`0.1`$ and a constant learning-rate schedule (cosine on Science Q&A).
Weight decay is $`0.01`$ for off-policy FKL on Science Q&A and $`0`$ for
the other Science Q&A methods.
Table [4](#A2.T4 "Table 4 ‣ B.3 Hyperparameter search ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
gives the per-method search grids. We select by accuracy on the task’s
held-out split
(Table [3](#A2.T3 "Table 3 ‣ B.2 Datasets, evaluation, and supervised-token accounting ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
SSD additionally selects $`D_{\mathrm{switch}}`$ and $`\tau`$. Learning
rate $`5\times 10^{-5}`$ wins for every method. Batch size $`32`$ wins
for the off-policy methods and $`8`$ for on-policy and SSD; the runs in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
use batch size $`8`$ for every method so that all curves share one step
size (141 optimizer steps per epoch on Company Memo and Wikipedia, 334
on Science Q&A). The selected switch is JSD with $`\tau=0.30`$ on
Company Memo and $`\tau=0.50`$ on Wikipedia, and reverse KL with
$`\tau=1.0`$ on Science Q&A. In
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
the off-policy runs iterate on their once-sampled targets for at least
the SSD training time and are shown up to the on-policy token budget.
Each selected configuration is trained with three seeds, and
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
reports the mean.

### B.4 Training infrastructure and decoding

The experiments in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
ran on NVIDIA A100-SXM4 80 GB GPUs: one GPU for the on-policy and
off-policy baselines, and a second GPU for the resident teacher worker
of SSD. The remaining experiments used NVIDIA H100 80 GB GPUs, including
four GPUs per run for the Qwen3-14B scaling experiment
(Appendix [B.5](#A2.SS5 "B.5 Larger-model scaling ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
We built our codebase on top of the SDFT codebase
([http://idanshenfeld.com/SDFT](http://idanshenfeld.com/SDFT)); training
is implemented on top of the TRL training engine ([von Werra et al.,
2020](#bib.bib40)), and online inference for both rollouts and judging
uses vLLM ([Kwon et al., 2023](#bib.bib23)). For training rollouts, we
set temperature $`=1.0`$, top-$`k=20`$, and top-$`p=1.0`$ across all the
baselines.
````
