### B.6 Forgetting experiment protocol

#### Setup.

We fine-tune Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the SciKnowEval Chemistry-L3
split used by [Shenfeld et al. (2026a)](#bib.bib35), consisting of 2,674
training examples and a 507-question held-out multiple-choice set for
in-domain Science Q&A (SciQA). Student and teacher are initialized from
the same base model. We report in-domain SciQA accuracy and
general-capability forgetting, measured as the mean accuracy change
across six standard benchmarks relative to the base model.

#### Training.

All methods use the shared training configuration in
Table [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Training. ‣ B.6 Forgetting experiment protocol ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").
We sweep learning rate for all methods and, for SSD, the JSD routing
threshold, selecting configurations by accuracy on the held-out SciQA
questions. SciQA is in-domain in the sense that these questions come
from the same task as the training set; the six general benchmarks are
never used for selection. The methods differ in rollout source, loss,
and routing. Off-policy (SFT) trains with cross-entropy on fixed
teacher-generated targets, while Off-policy (FKL) uses forward KL to the
frozen teacher distribution on the same targets with softmax temperature
$`T=1.0`$. On-policy and SSD use the reasoning-prompt format, where the
model emits \<reasoning\>…\</reasoning\> followed by \<answer\>.
On-policy applies forward KL on student-sampled rollouts. SSD uses
mixed-policy rollouts with per-token JSD switching at threshold
$`\tau=0.2`$.

|  |  |
|----|----|
| Hyperparameter | Value |
| Epochs | 2 |
| Effective batch size | 16 |
| Learning rate schedule | cosine, 1.5% warmup |
| Gradient clipping | 1.0 |
| Precision | bf16 |
| Learning rate | $`5{\times}10^{-5}`$, except SSD uses $`3{\times}10^{-5}`$ |
| Completion length | 2048 tokens for rollout-based methods |
| Loss-token mask | first 5 tokens for rollout-based methods |

Table 6: Shared training configuration for the forgetting experiments.

#### Evaluation.

We evaluate general-capability retention with the EleutherAI
lm-evaluation-harness ([Gao et al., 2024a](#bib.bib8)), pinned to the
SDFT-paper commit 03c44adc ([Shenfeld et al., 2026a](#bib.bib35)), using
a vLLM backend ([Kwon et al., 2023](#bib.bib23)) with dtype=bfloat16,
gpu_memory_utilization=0.85, max_model_len=8192, and --batch_size auto.
Table [7](#A2.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Evaluation. ‣ B.6 Forgetting experiment protocol ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
lists the six forgetting benchmarks and metrics. We define Avg.6 as
their unweighted mean and
$`\Delta=\text{Avg.6}-\text{Avg.6}(\text{base})`$. SciQA is evaluated
separately on the 507-question holdout by exact match on the extracted
\<answer\> letter, generating up to 2048 tokens.

|            |                            |                              |
|------------|----------------------------|------------------------------|
| Task       | Metric                     | Scoring                      |
| HellaSwag  | acc, not length-normalized | loglikelihood, deterministic |
| MMLU       | acc                        | loglikelihood, deterministic |
| TruthfulQA | mc1                        | loglikelihood, deterministic |
| Winogrande | acc                        | loglikelihood, deterministic |
| HumanEval  | pass@1                     | generative, greedy           |
| IFEval     | inst_level_loose_acc       | generative, greedy           |

Table 7: Forgetting benchmarks and metrics.

#### Confidence intervals.

For SciQA, we report the mean and 95% Student’s $`t`$ confidence
interval across three sampled decodes at temperature $`T=0.7`$.

### B.7 Paired teacher–student inference engine

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 8: Paired vLLM inference for SSD. The teacher and student run on
separate GPUs with different prefixes and a shared continuation. At each
token, the teacher sends its hidden state to the student GPU through
NCCL. Both output heads, the switching test, and sampling run on the
student GPU. The selected token is written into both models’ request
histories, with NCCL carrying it back to the teacher. CPU code launches
each decode step and reads back token IDs every eight steps.

We implemented SSD with two vLLM ([Kwon et al., 2023](#bib.bib23))
workers, one for the teacher and one for the student, each on a separate
GPU. A CPU controller admits batches and supplies the student prefix
$`x`$ and the teacher prefix $`[C;x]`$, where $`C`$ is the additional
context available to the teacher. Each worker maintains its own model
weights and KV cache. We use vLLM’s internal GPU worker and Model Runner
V2 to run the models, with our own scheduling, routing, and sampling
code. This adapter leaves the installed vLLM source unchanged.
Figure [8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ B.7 Paired teacher–student inference engine ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
shows the inference data flow.

In our configuration, both workers prefill their prefixes, and then
generate a shared continuation. At position $`t`$, both models condition
on the same previously selected tokens $`y_{<t}`$. The teacher sends its
final post-normalization hidden state $`h^{T}_{t}`$ to the student GPU
through NCCL. On the student GPU, we project $`h^{T}_{t}`$ with a
resident copy of the teacher’s output head and $`h^{S}_{t}`$ with the
student’s head. We compare the logits using the switch rule and select
the model and sample one token $`y_{t}`$ from the selected distribution.
The student worker sends $`y_{t}`$ to the teacher through NCCL, and both
workers write it into vLLM’s request state on the GPU before the next
forward pass.

For Qwen3-4B, sending hidden states limits the teacher-to-student
transfer to $`2{,}560`$ values per active request and token, compared
with $`151{,}936`$ values for a full logit vector. Routing, sampling,
token exchange, and token-history updates stay on the GPUs. Keeping the
selected tokens on the GPUs lets us launch the next decode step without
waiting for those tokens to be copied back to the CPU. CPU workers
prepare metadata and launch each decode step. They read back token IDs
every eight steps. The parent controller receives the completed
admission batch. With CUDA graphs enabled, we replay both vLLM decode
bodies and the custom projection and routing head. We compile the
divergence computation to fuse its elementwise operations and
reductions. At admission, we reserve KV-cache pages for each prompt and
its full continuation budget to avoid capacity-driven preemption,
eviction, and re-prefill within the batch.

In the resident training configuration, the teacher worker keeps the
hidden states used to predict the generated tokens on its GPU. The
trainer imports them through CUDA IPC, with one device-to-device copy
per admission group into its own storage. It projects the cached states
with the teacher head to compute the forward-KL targets. This avoids a
second teacher forward pass and storing full-vocabulary logits for the
whole sequence. With sufficient GPU memory, the student’s training
weights, gradients, and optimizer state stay on the same GPU as the
student vLLM worker, and both inference workers remain resident between
rollout and training phases.

### B.8 Training time per supervised token

We profile Qwen3-4B on Science Q&A over three training seeds. For each
seed, we divide mean phase time per step by mean supervised tokens per
step, convert to minutes per million tokens, and average across seeds
(Table [8](#A2.T8 "Table 8 ‣ B.8 Training time per supervised token ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).
Token counts follow
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2.SSS0.Px1 "Supervised tokens. ‣ B.2 Datasets, evaluation, and supervised-token accounting ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"),
including each reuse of an off-policy target. GPU allocations are
described in
Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Training infrastructure and decoding ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Method | Generation |     Loss  calculation | Backward |     Update  + sync | Other | Total |
| SSD | 30.25 | 3.16 | 6.37 | 0.50 | 1.10 | 41.38 |
| On-policy | 28.86 | 5.64 | 5.64 | 0.23 | 1.16 | 41.54 |
| Off-policy FKL | 0.00 | 4.01 | 6.26 | 0.19 | 0.80 | 11.25 |
| Off-policy SFT | 0.00 | 2.47 | 5.41 | 0.15 | 0.67 | 8.71 |

Table 8: Training-phase wall time in minutes per million supervised
tokens on Science Q&A, excluding offline target generation.

Generation includes rollout computation and bookkeeping. Loss
calculation includes training forward passes, target preparation, and
loss arithmetic. Update + sync combines gradient clipping, the optimizer
update, and measured weight synchronization to rollout workers, which we
subtract from generation. Other is the residual step time, including
unassigned data-loading, callback, and synchronization overhead.
Evaluation and checkpoint saving are excluded.

SSD and on-policy training take nearly the same wall time per supervised
token with these GPU allocations. SSD decodes with the teacher on its
second GPU concurrently with the student and reuses cached teacher
hidden states in the loss phase. The shorter loss phase offsets its
higher generation and backward times per token. Reaching matched
accuracy with fewer tokens therefore shortens training
(Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 SSD’s token savings translate into faster training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")).

Off-policy training has no in-step generation. Sampling its teacher
targets once takes approximately 9.5 minutes per run, which is included
separately in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 SSD’s token savings translate into faster training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").
Amortized over all recorded training tokens, this adds approximately
0.33 minutes per million tokens for FKL and 0.22 for SFT. These
amortized costs depend on how many times the targets are reused.

## Appendix C Additional Analyses

These experiments probe where the supervision signal goes, how SSD
compares with retrieval at inference time, and how the choice of
switching rule matters.

### C.1 Supervision-signal measurements

These experiments support the analysis in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 The Inefficiency of On-Policy Self-Distillation ‣ 3 Speculative Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
by examining how the source of a rollout affects the supervision it
provides. We ask whether teacher-generated trajectories provide stronger
feedback than student-generated trajectories, and whether feedback
weakens as a student rollout grows longer. The Wikipedia comparison
addresses both questions, while the Science Q&A analysis checks the
positional pattern on longer responses. In both experiments, we measure
supervision with forward KL from the privileged teacher to the student,
matching the distillation loss.

On Wikipedia,
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Dense supervision versus rollout intervention. ‣ 2 A Unified View of Self-Distillation ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
compares single on-policy and off-policy training runs of Qwen3-4B with
a frozen teacher. Both train for eight epochs; off-policy training
reuses teacher answers sampled once per question. Off-policy training
reaches $`78\%`$ accuracy with roughly five times fewer supervised
tokens, while on-policy training reaches higher final accuracy. The
positional analysis uses the untrained student on all 1,129 training
questions, comparing teacher-written answers with greedy student
rollouts capped at 128 tokens. On student-generated prefixes, mean
per-token loss falls from roughly $`1.5`$–$`2.0`$ at early positions to
about $`0.5`$ by position 75, while teacher-generated prefixes retain a
higher signal over the plotted range. Means include only rollouts that
reach each position, and shaded bands show 90% bootstrap intervals over
questions.

On Science Q&A, we examine the same on-policy signal along longer
responses, using 256 rollouts from the untrained student, one per
question, capped at 1024 tokens. Feedback weakens later in the response:
the mean signal in the first quartile is $`3.3\times`$ that in the last.
Beyond position 512, it falls to about one-seventeenth of its value at
positions 5–8. As on Wikipedia, positional means include only rollouts
that reach each position.

The concentration of teacher–student disagreement early in on-policy
rollouts is consistent with the motivation for SSD: as student errors
accumulate, the rollout may enter prefixes where the teacher provides
weaker corrective feedback. We therefore switch to the teacher at
positions of high disagreement. In standard on-policy training, later
tokens still receive the dense distillation loss but provide weaker
feedback. SSD applies the same dense loss, using teacher interventions
to keep rollouts closer to teacher-generated trajectories and preserve
stronger supervision.

### C.2 Retrieved-demonstration comparison

The main experiments ask whether self-distillation can store new
knowledge in the model’s parameters so that it can answer questions
without privileged context at test time. Retrieval provides a natural
alternative: keep the knowledge external and supply related solved
examples in the inference prompt. To contextualize the closed-book
results, we compare SSD with retrieved demonstrations on Science Q&A at
4B and 14B scales.

For each evaluation question, we retrieve four training questions
together with their reference answers and insert them as solved
demonstrations. BM25 uses lexical similarity, while dense retrieval uses
cosine similarity under Qwen3-Embedding-4B. We evaluate both retrieval
methods, the unaugmented closed-book base model, and the closed-book SSD
model using the same answer extraction. Generated-token counts include
only the response, not the retrieved prompt.

We evaluate the final SSD checkpoints. The Qwen3-4B results average the
three Science Q&A training seeds shown in
Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 SSD’s token savings translate into faster training ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization");
the Qwen3-14B results use the run reported in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").
Generation limits are given in
Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Training infrastructure and decoding ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization").

|           |                            |          |                       |
|-----------|----------------------------|----------|-----------------------|
| Model     | Inference method           | Accuracy | Mean generated tokens |
| Qwen3-4B  | Closed-book base           | 49.9     | 2864                  |
| Qwen3-4B  | Top-4 BM25 demonstrations  | 65.9     | 2045                  |
| Qwen3-4B  | Top-4 dense demonstrations | 61.3     | 2146                  |
| Qwen3-4B  | SSD closed-book            | 66.3     | 508                   |
| Qwen3-14B | Closed-book base           | 45.2     | 373                   |
| Qwen3-14B | Top-4 BM25 demonstrations  | 58.4     | 510                   |
| Qwen3-14B | Top-4 dense demonstrations | 55.6     | 465                   |
| Qwen3-14B | SSD closed-book            | 75.5     | 222                   |

Table 9: Closed-book internalization compared with retrieved
demonstrations on Science Q&A. BM25 and dense retrieval supply four
solved training questions; SSD receives only the test question. Base and
retrieval responses are capped at $`16384`$ tokens; SSD responses are
capped at $`1024`$ tokens for Qwen3-4B and $`2048`$ tokens for
Qwen3-14B. Mean generated-token counts cover responses only, excluding
the prompt.

Retrieval improves the untrained model at both scales, confirming that
relevant solved examples help on this task. Nevertheless, closed-book
SSD matches or exceeds the strongest retrieved-demonstration baseline
while producing much shorter responses. This comparison does not
establish that parametric internalization is generally preferable to
retrieval: the retriever selects solved training questions rather than
raw source documents.

### C.3 Switching-rule ablation

Table [10](#A3.T10 "Table 10 ‣ C.3 Switching-rule ablation ‣ Appendix C Additional Analyses ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
asks whether SSD needs to compare the full teacher and student
distributions, or whether simpler token-level signals from prior work
are sufficient. To isolate the switching rule, the ablation holds the
model, data, loss, learning rate, schedule, and training seed fixed on
Science Q&A. All ablation runs use an effective batch size of 16 and
train for two epochs with a cosine learning-rate schedule and $`1.5\%`$
warmup. We evaluate each run’s final checkpoint with three sampled
decodes at temperature $`0.3`$.

We compare five rules. Following Speculative Knowledge Distillation
(SKD) ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)), the top-$`k`$ rule first samples
a student proposal and lets the teacher emit the token when that
proposal falls outside the teacher’s top-$`k`$ candidates. The entropy
rule, loosely motivated by entropy-aware on-policy distillation ([Jin
et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)), which uses teacher entropy to adapt the
loss, switches the rollout on student entropy with threshold $`2.0`$.
The three distribution-level switches use JSD ($`\tau=0.25`$), reverse
KL ($`\tau=1.0`$), and forward KL ($`\tau=0.5`$). Because these
statistics have different numerical scales, we compare the rules through
the realized fraction of tokens emitted by the teacher. As in the
Science Q&A runs of
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"),
the teacher in these runs is an exponential moving average of the
student with mixing rate $`0.01`$.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Switching rule | Setting | Teacher-token frac. | Accuracy | Tokens (M) |
| JSD | $`\tau=0.25`$ | 0.7% | $`63.3\pm 3.4`$ | 4.47 |
| Top-$`k`$ inclusion | $`k=1`$ | 9.3% | $`62.0\pm 2.0`$ | 4.51 |
| Entropy | $`\tau=2.0`$ | 11.5% | $`59.2\pm 1.2`$ | 5.18 |
| Reverse KL, $`D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{T})`$ | $`\tau=1.0`$ | 1.5% | $`65.2\pm 0.3`$ | 4.02 |
| Forward KL, $`D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{T}\,\|\,\pi_{\theta})`$ | $`\tau=0.5`$ | 3.4% | $`\mathbf{67.0\pm 3.1}`$ | 4.07 |

Table 10: Switching-rule ablation on Science Q&A. All rows share the
training configuration, seed, and forward-KL loss; only the switching
rule changes. Accuracy is the mean and 95% confidence interval over
three sampled decodes. Teacher-token fraction is the fraction of rollout
positions generated by the teacher at the end of training.

For the top-$`k`$ rule we sweep $`k\in\{20,5,1\}`$. The student’s
proposal already lies within the teacher’s top-20 candidates at
$`99.7\%`$ of positions and within its top-5 at $`98.5\%`$, so these two
settings almost never invoke the teacher and reduce to nearly on-policy
generation;
Table [10](#A3.T10 "Table 10 ‣ C.3 Switching-rule ablation ‣ Appendix C Additional Analyses ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
therefore reports the non-degenerate $`k=1`$ setting. Even this setting
and the entropy rule reach lower mean accuracy than switching on JSD,
forward KL, or reverse KL, consistent with prior work using
distribution-level disagreement for adaptive switching ([Peng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib32); [Koo et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)). These results
suggest that the context can substantially redistribute probability mass
without moving the student’s proposal outside the teacher’s top-$`k`$.
The three distribution-level switches perform similarly, with
overlapping intervals, and in this single-seed comparison we see no
clear difference among them: the intervals are over three decodes of one
training seed, and the rules fire at different teacher fractions
($`0.7\%`$ to $`11.5\%`$), so the rows are not matched on teacher share.
We use JSD as the default because its $`\ln 2`$ upper bound puts
$`\tau`$ on a fixed, interpretable scale; the Science Q&A runs of
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2 SSD reaches on-policy accuracy with fewer supervised tokens ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
use the reverse-KL switch.

## Appendix D Case Study: JSD-Routed Inference on SciKnowEval Chemistry-L3

### D.1 Setup

We evaluate offline how the JSD routing threshold qualitatively changes
rollouts on the 507-question SciKnowEval Chemistry-L3 multiple-choice
evaluation set. No weights are trained. Instead, at each decoding step
we run two forward passes of the same Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 checkpoint:
a student pass conditioned only on the question, and a teacher pass
conditioned on the question plus privileged context containing the
ground-truth answer. We then route each generated token according to the
JSD between the two next-token distributions. This isolates how changing
the routing threshold $`\tau`$ changes which tokens come from the
teacher and how those interventions alter the resulting rollout.
Decoding is capped at $`1024`$ tokens, and a response that reaches the
cap without an answer tag is scored as incorrect; this is why the
student-only accuracy here ($`12.8\%`$) is lower than the closed-book
base accuracy in
Table [9](#A3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ C.2 Retrieved-demonstration comparison ‣ Appendix C Additional Analyses ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization"),
which uses a $`16384`$-token budget.

### D.2 Aggregate sweep

Table [11](#A4.T11 "Table 11 ‣ D.2 Aggregate sweep ‣ Appendix D Case Study: JSD-Routed Inference on SciKnowEval Chemistry-L3 ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
summarizes the sweep.

|                   |        |            |               |
|-------------------|--------|------------|---------------|
| Strategy          | Acc.   | Mean resp. | Teacher frac. |
|                   |        | length     | (per-row)     |
| Student only      | 12.8%  | 879        | 00.0%         |
| SSD, $`\tau=0.6`$ | 34.12% | 850        | 01.3%         |
| SSD, $`\tau=0.5`$ | 51.87% | 745        | 02.7%         |
| SSD, $`\tau=0.3`$ | 66.07% | 588        | 07.0%         |
| SSD, $`\tau=0.1`$ | 73.96% | 523        | 15.7%         |
| Teacher only      | 80.28% | 487        | 100.0%        |

Table 11: JSD-routed inference on SciKnowEval Chemistry-L3. Routed
decoding recovers most of the teacher’s accuracy while using only a
small fraction of teacher tokens.

At $`\tau=0.1`$, only $`15.7\%`$ of tokens per question come from the
teacher on average, yet accuracy reaches $`73.96\%`$, within roughly six
percentage points of the pure-teacher ceiling. This supports the central
intuition behind SSD: teacher signal is often concentrated at a small
number of decisive positions.

### D.3 Qualitative case study

We now show a representative synthesis question.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Option B contains the exact product fragment OCCN1CCN(CC(F)(F)F)CC1
attached to a TIPS silyl protecting group, so removing the silyl ether
yields the product.

Table [12](#A4.T12 "Table 12 ‣ D.3 Qualitative case study ‣ Appendix D Case Study: JSD-Routed Inference on SciKnowEval Chemistry-L3 ‣ Speculative Self-Distillation enables Efficient Knowledge Internalization")
summarizes the single-example behavior. In the rollouts below,
coral-highlighted spans were emitted from the teacher distribution;
unhighlighted text was emitted from the student distribution. Token
boundaries follow the model’s BPE, and \n denotes a newline. The
provenance trails come from a single-prompt deterministic rerun, so the
exact routing differs slightly from the batched aggregate sweep, but the
qualitative behavior is the same.

|                   |                |               |        |           |
|-------------------|----------------|---------------|--------|-----------|
| Strategy          | Teacher tokens | Teacher frac. | Length | Extracted |
| Student only      | 0              | 0.0%          | 1024   | no tag    |
| SSD, $`\tau=0.6`$ | 11             | 1.1%          | 1024   | no tag    |
| SSD, $`\tau=0.5`$ | 4              | 0.4%          | 1024   | no tag    |
| SSD, $`\tau=0.3`$ | 9              | 0.9%          | 1024   | no tag    |
| SSD, $`\tau=0.1`$ | 75             | 9.0%          | 837    | B         |
| Teacher only      | 549            | 100.0%        | 549    | B         |

Table 12: Single-question JSD-routed rollouts. In this single-prompt
rerun, only $`\tau=0.1`$ routes enough teacher tokens to escape the
student’s parsing loop and produce the correct answer. The teacher count
does not fall steadily as $`\tau`$ grows: each teacher token changes the
text that every later step conditions on, so the runs see different
prefixes after their first switch.

#### Student-only: recursive parsing failure.

The student repeatedly reparses the target SMILES string and reaches the
1024-token budget without emitting an answer.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Moderate thresholds: small nudges are insufficient.

At $`\tau=0.6`$, $`\tau=0.5`$, and $`\tau=0.3`$, the teacher fires on a
small number of framing tokens. This changes the opening of the
response, but in this single-prompt run it does not redirect the model
enough to produce an answer before the token budget.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Low threshold: routing changes the strategy.

At $`\tau=0.1`$, teacher routing covers a denser set of setup tokens.
The rollout moves from recursive SMILES parsing to the correct
structural-motif strategy: identify which answer choice contains the
product fragment.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Teacher-only.

The teacher-only rollout is correct and shorter. Since every token is
generated from the privileged-context distribution, we do not highlight
each token individually.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The visible pattern is that teacher routing fires on framing and setup
tokens, not on the answer letter itself. The student-only rollout opens
by trying to parse the SMILES string and gets stuck in a loop. Moderate
thresholds insert a few teacher tokens, such as “The”, quote marks, and
small structural tokens, which weakly shift the framing but do not
change the outcome. At $`\tau=0.1`$, teacher routing covers enough of
the setup to move the rollout into the correct strategy: analyze the
product, identify the shared structural motif, and choose the option
containing that motif.
